one_liner: Tiny Go xorshift32 PRNG with a sync.Pool of generators; out-scaled the mutex-locked global math/rand under parallel load.
what_it_does: Provides goroutine-safe package functions Uint32() and Uint32n(maxN) plus an unsynchronized RNG type with Uint32, Uint32n and Seed. The package functions borrow an RNG from a sync.Pool, draw one number and return it, so many goroutines can call them without sharing a lock. The API covers only uint32 output; there is no Int63, Float64, Intn, Shuffle, Perm or Read, so it does not replace math/rand.
how_it_is_fast: The generator is Marsaglia's 32-bit xorshift (shifts 13, 17, 5) on a 4-byte state, and bounded values use Lemire's multiply-shift reduction ((x * maxN) >> 32) with no division or rejection loop. The scaling comes from the sync.Pool: each P tends to reuse its own pooled RNG, avoiding the single mutex that guarded the global math/rand source in Go versions before 1.21. The per-goroutine RNG path (6.50 ns/op at GOMAXPROCS=1) is cheaper again because it skips the pool Get/Put.
when_to_use: Legacy Go code pinned to Go 1.20 or older that calls top-level math/rand functions from many goroutines and spends measurable time contending on the global generator's lock.
Hot loops needing cheap bounded uint32 values for non-security decisions: random load-balancer or shard selection, sampling, jitter, test data.
Single-goroutine or per-worker code that can own a fastrand.RNG value, where a 4-byte xorshift state and a multiply-shift bound are good enough.
As a reference for the pool-of-generators pattern if you must vendor something very small (about 80 lines, MIT).
when_not_to_use: Go 1.21 and later: unseeded top-level math/rand functions already use a lock-free fastSource that calls the runtime's per-M wyrand (fastrand64), so the multi-CPU contention this package fixes is gone; prefer the standard library or math/rand/v2 there. No benchmark of fastrand against Go 1.21+ math/rand exists.
Anything security-related: the package doc says to use crypto/rand for cryptographically secure numbers, and seeds come from the wall clock.

Simulation or statistics work: a 32-bit xorshift on 4 bytes of state has period at most 2^32-1, small next to the 64-bit and larger generators in this category; Uint32n's multiply-shift without rejection is slightly biased whenever maxN is not a power of two.

Reproducible streams from the global functions: pooled generators are created and reseeded from the clock whenever the pool is empty (sync.Pool can drop objects at garbage collection), so sequences cannot be replayed.
Code needing floats, 64-bit integers, shuffles or other distributions; only uint32 output is offered.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library sync and time only)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; go.mod declares only the module path with no go directive (Go modules support was added in 2019)
integration.platforms: any platform Go supports (pure Go, no assembly)
integration.thread_safety: Package-level Uint32 and Uint32n are documented as safe from concurrent goroutines; RNG methods are documented as unsafe for concurrent use.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — Uint32n(n) can replace rand.Int31n(n) call sites for non-negative bounds, but the function names, uint32 types and missing methods (Int63, Float64, Intn, Shuffle, Seed on the global stream) mean it is not a drop-in replacement for math/rand.

gotchas: Seeds come from time.Now().UnixNano() folded to 32 bits when a pooled RNG is first used; open issue #4 (2021) notes that many goroutines starting together can get identically seeded generators on systems with coarse clock resolution, and that the pool holds one RNG per concurrent caller rather than strictly one per CPU.
RNG.Seed(0) does not give a fixed stream: a zero state is treated as unseeded and is replaced by a clock-derived seed on the next call.
Uint32n has no argument check: Uint32n(0) silently returns 0.

The README benchmark at GOMAXPROCS=1 shows only a small gain for the global function (29.7 vs 31.8 ns/op); most of the single-thread gain is from owning an RNG (6.50 ns/op), which you could equally get by owning a rand.New(...) source (17.9 ns/op) or a faster per-goroutine generator.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among Go siblings, pgregory.net/rand (flyingmutant/rand) is maintained, offers the full math/rand-style API on sfc64 and benchmarks against math/rand/v2, and vpxyz/xorshift offers stronger 64-bit xorshift/xoroshiro sources; pick valyala/fastrand only when you need a tiny vendored uint32 helper on an old Go toolchain, and lukechampine/frand when you need cryptographic strength.
verified_claims_summary: The README's go test -bench output (goos linux, goarch amd64; CPU and Go version not stated; results committed in April 2017) uses b.RunParallel loops drawing bounded values below 1e6: fastrand.Uint32n took 29.7, 17.6 and 14.2 ns/op versus math/rand's global Int31n at 31.8, 51.2 and 145 ns/op at GOMAXPROCS=1, 2 and 4, and a per-goroutine RNG.Uint32n took 6.50, 3.36 and 3.30 ns/op versus a per-goroutine rand.New(rand.NewSource(42)).Int31n at 17.9, 11.0 and 8.35 ns/op. The global-function gap measured lock contention in pre-Go 1.21 math/rand, which Go 1.21 removed for unseeded programs.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit 2021-09-15 (RNG.Seed), issue #4 open since 2021 with no reply, and four contributor PRs (crypto/rand seeding, go.mod version, sync.Pool New, test fix) closed unmerged in April 2024; MIT and small enough to vendor, but on Go 1.21+ the standard library makes it largely unnecessary.
